observations.quote: Of that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers
observations.what: that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers
observations.note: The chapter heading names its subject as one single chief Medicine and gives it to the most ancient philosophers.

observations.quote: This occult Minerva of Phylosophy & this only most precious Jewell is inestimable.
observations.what: This occult Minerva of Phylosophy & this only most precious Jewell
observations.note: The margin gives the subject two further names, an occult Minerva of philosophy and the only most precious Jewell, and calls it beyond price; 'occult' marks it hidden.

observations.quote: I shall here supply what yet pertaineth to that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
observations.what: that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
observations.note: The chapter's subject is named again as one chief and universal philosophical physick; the wording ('what yet pertaineth to that') treats it as a thing already spoken of.

observations.quote: than which a greater gift of wisdom we never read that divine bounty bestowed on man
observations.note: Croll holds that no greater gift of wisdom was ever given to man.

observations.quote: this most secret Secret of secret Secrets, by which even wonders, yea all things may be done
observations.what: this most secret Secret of secret Secrets
observations.note: The same thing is named the most secret Secret of secret Secrets; the heaped word marks it as hidden above all else, and all things are said to be done by it.

observations.quote: the Plannets of inferior Astronomy, whose imperfection and drosse it causeth to vanish by piercing them with its most powerfull impressions
observations.note: Planets of an 'inferior Astronomy' have imperfection and dross that the medicine removes. Interpreted (the readers' inference): the parenthesis that follows names 'metallick and Humane bodies', so these planets most narrowly stand for the metallic bodies; the text does not state the equation itself.

observations.quote: it segregateth all extraneous Sulphureity and impure Terrestreity from metallick and Humane bodies
observations.note: What the medicine does: it separates foreign sulphureity and impure earthiness from metallic and human bodies alike.

observations.quote: the recovering covering and preserving of the languishing and lost health of the Human body, by its fiery vigour
observations.note: A second use: it restores and preserves human health, by a 'fiery vigour'. The doubled 'recovering covering' stands so in the text.

observations.quote: to say nothing now of the Magicall and super Celestial use
observations.note: Croll names a magical and super-celestial use and says he passes it over here.

observations.quote: when the Gonetick influence of the beames of the Sun and Moon and the fourth revolution is finisht upon its native Earth
observations.note: A condition for that further use: the influence of the beams of Sun and Moon, and a fourth revolution finished upon 'its native Earth'. The lines given do not say what the revolution or the native Earth are.

observations.quote: John Dee of London, and Roger Bacon
observations.name: John Dee of London; Roger Bacon
observations.note: Beside the words on the fourth revolution and the thing's influential power, the margin sends the reader to a writing of John Dee of London (its title partly illegible, 'Mo...ade') and to Roger Bacon.

observations.quote: it is endowed absolutly with all created Influentiall power as well in the Elementall world, as in the Celestiall or super celestiall
observations.note: Once that revolution is finished, the thing is said to hold all created influential power in three worlds: elemental, celestial, super-celestial.

observations.quote: so doth he usually hide his wonderfull Gifts in wonderfull men
observations.note: God is said to hide his wonderful gifts in wonderful men: the gift is lodged in persons, not openly given.

observations.quote: the consent of all those most learned men who in every age have lived with the greatest admiration and prayse of many, do bear witnesse that this is so
observations.note: Croll rests the claim on all antiquity, the tradition of all nations and languages, the consent of learned men of every age, and the 'ocular inspectation and certification of many of our time'.

observations.quote: their writings, which are woven of so many Hieroglyphicall, Magicall, and Mathematicall Coverings
observations.note: The writings of those learned men are said to be woven of hieroglyphical, magical and mathematical coverings: their truth is given under covers.

observations.quote: doth warrant and assure a removall of old age and renewing of youth, perpetuall health, and honest food and rayment
observations.note: What the gift is said to assure: old age removed, youth renewed, lasting health, honest food and clothing.

observations.quote: to the Pious and holy Phylosophers dignified by Nature and Education
observations.note: The assurance is given only to pious and holy philosophers fitted by nature and education.

observations.quote: not by usury and fraud, nor cheating wares, nor by oppression of the poor (as most of our rich men are now inriched) but by industry of work and labour of the hands
observations.note: The living it gives comes by work of the hands, set against usury, fraud and oppression, by which Croll says most rich men of his time grow rich.

observations.quote: God forbid therefore, that, sleighting the example of the Ancients, I should either deny such precious Wonders of GOD, and darken the wonderfull powers of Nature
observations.note: Croll refuses to deny these wonders, to darken the powers of Nature, or to revile them as most do.

observations.quote: as if they were but the speculations of idle men, or the empty dreams and fictions of a sottish and doting mind
observations.name: the most
observations.note: The view of those who revile these wonders ('as the most doe'), reported in order to reject it: that they are idle speculation, dream and fiction.

observations.quote: whom the Phylosophers call fools
observations.name: Phylosophers
observations.note: The name 'fools' for those who revile and do not know is given as the philosophers' word.

observations.quote: are not to be admitted to them, those also that dote in their Phantasticall dreams are utterly to be excluded
observations.note: The gift is called 'divine Banquets', and two kinds are shut out of it: the revilers who do not know it, and those who dote in fantastical dreams.

observations.quote: Here some are listning, whether trusting to my own ingenuity I dare boast also of the preparation hereof in this place
observations.note: Croll says some wait to hear whether he will here claim the preparation of the medicine; the following paragraphs answer by declining to falsify, and the margin casts him only as a pointer of the way.

observations.quote: as those covètous Mountebanks and greedy Phylosophists use to doe
observations.note: Arrogating 'the absolute knowledge of this Art' for show is what covetous mountebanks and 'Phylosophists' do; Croll sets himself apart from them.

observations.quote: Here I would be taken as an Index, or as one standing at the door to direct others the way they should goe
observations.note: In the margin Croll names his role here: a pointer, or one at the door showing others the way, whom he may profit more than himself, and a whetstone to spur them on, rather than one who claims the Art.

observations.quote: because I promised the Courteous Reader a little before, that I would set down at least those things which I had made tryall of
observations.note: Points back to an earlier promise in this writing: to set down at least what he himself had tried.

observations.quote: to falsifie any thing concerning the undoubted certainty of this matter
observations.note: Croll will not falsify anything about this matter, whose certainty he calls undoubted; falsifying is the part of cheaters, not of a wise man.

observations.quote: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science, not of Sophisters, but Phylosophers
observations.what: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science
observations.note: The Art is named sacred and divine and set apart as that of philosophers, not of 'Sophisters'.

observations.quote: which the ignorant basely and wretchedly condemn of falshood
observations.name: the ignorant
observations.note: The charge of falsehood is given as the judgement of the ignorant, reported in order to reject it.

observations.quote: among all Arts, as well Liberall as Mechanick, none aboundeth with so many Imposters as this
observations.note: Croll grants that no art has as many impostors as this one, while holding it true.

observations.quote: to be preferred before all other earthly Sciences by those that are true Physitians
observations.note: True physicians should set this art above every other earthly science.

observations.quote: it cannot be that a poor or covetous man should spend his time in the study of Phylosophy
observations.note: A condition of the student: neither poor nor covetous, but content and furnished with honest food and clothing.

observations.quote: pray unto God after the example of Solomon, not for wealth, but wisdome, that he would open to them the Magazine of Divine knowledge
observations.note: The true physicians pray for wisdom and not wealth, Solomon named as their example (an example, not words given to him); they ask that God open 'the Magazine of Divine knowledge'.

observations.quote: the Magazine of Divine knowledge
observations.note: Divine knowledge is set as a store-house that God opens to those who pray.

observations.quote: who measure their happinesse at least by Heaven, and the Love of God the giver of every good thing
observations.note: A mark of the fit seekers: they measure happiness by Heaven and the love of God.

observations.quote: moved and spurred on to search it out by the love of Secrets and of Nature, according to the Divine Grace
observations.note: A further mark: they search from love of secrets and of Nature, under divine grace.

observations.quote: doe in the fear of God refuse no honest, constant and possible labor of the hands
observations.note: A further mark: seeking knowledge 'without any foolish hope of gaine or affectation of vaine glory', they refuse no honest, constant work of the hands.

observations.quote: By Wisdome the heart is made constant.
observations.note: A saying in the margin beside the words on constant labour: wisdom makes the heart constant. The note names no source.

observations.quote: that End which belongs to the Master of Nature, to wit, the Praise and Honour of God, and the good of his needy neighbor
observations.note: Stated: the text glosses 'that End' itself with 'to wit': the gifts are to be used for the praise and honour of God and the good of the needy neighbour.

observations.quote: in a constant Taciturnity, without pride, which provoketh the envy of all men
observations.note: The gifts are to be used in constant silence, without the pride that stirs envy.

observations.quote: They that carry about their Treasure and use it publickly. Job 22.25.
observations.name: Job
observations.note: The margin at the head of the paragraph speaks of those who carry their treasure about and use it openly, and cites Job 22.25.

observations.quote: among the Children of the golden doctrine (whose gold is the Omnipotent God)
observations.note: Stated: the text glosses the 'gold' of the golden doctrine as God himself, so 'golden' is not said plainly of metal here.

observations.quote: that most rare Good, which is to be prefer'd before all riches, is justly and of right to be searched out for the health sake of men
observations.note: By the seekers just described the rare good is rightly sought, and for the sake of men's health.

observations.quote: leaving the mettalls to those who with an impious hunger, and a thirsty and insatiable desire of being rich
observations.note: Such seekers leave 'the mettalls' to those driven by the desire of riches, who torment themselves night and day at risk of body and soul.

observations.quote: A Phylosopher must covet Nothing but Wisdome, which is conversant about Divine things
observations.note: Croll's rule: the philosopher desires only wisdom, which concerns divine things; a true philosopher never sought riches but delights in the mysteries of Nature.

observations.quote: he that is adept or hath attained the same may carry about with him in his purse, not the worth of one Kingdom only, but the wealth almost of the whole World
observations.note: The one who has attained it can carry almost the whole world's wealth in his purse, though he does not seek riches; 'adept' is set beside 'hath attained the same'.

observations.quote: either by the immediate inspiration of the most High, or by the expert ocular demonstration of a wise Master in this Art
observations.note: The gift is gained in two ways only, not by wrath or force: direct inspiration from God, or a wise master's demonstration seen with the eyes.

observations.quote: That without all controversie this is so, no man that doth apply himselfe to Phylosophy will deny.
observations.note: Croll holds that no student of philosophy denies this.

observations.quote: But who among many thousands is it, who while he seeketh this very knowledge by a certaine and subduing judgement and due means
observations.note: Croll asks who among many thousands of seekers reaches it; the question implies very few.

observations.quote: passe thorow the porch and gate of the Heavens into the Oratory or Chappell of Apollo, and get to the top of the mount of Chymistry
observations.note: Attaining the knowledge by another's help is put as passing the gate of the heavens into Apollo's chapel and climbing the mount of Chymistry: figures of place, not explained in these lines.

observations.quote: who durst lend a hand to another herein, except he hat for a long time, and by much experience known him
observations.note: No one dares help another to the secret unless long experience has shown him eminent in fear of God, holiness of life and 'pure and Harpocraticall Faith'.

observations.quote: pure and Harpocraticall Faith
observations.note: The faith required is called 'Harpocraticall'. Interpreted (reader A's): it joins the demand of 'constant Taciturnity' in CH6.10; the lines do not explain the word.

observations.quote: But where is that Aegyptian Bird to be found, that we may commend such a Phaenix?
observations.note: The margin calls the person so proved an Egyptian bird, a Phaenix, and asks where such a one is found: one hardly to be found.

observations.quote: See Paracel. in his fragments of Physick, which are to be refer'd to the 4 Tome fol. 311.
observations.name: Paracel.
observations.note: The margin points to Paracel.'s fragments of physick, fourth tome, folio 311, beside this passage.

observations.quote: that hath the Secret, & teacheth it while he liveth
observations.note: Entrance is only by divine revelation or by word of mouth (printed 'month') from one who has the Secret and teaches it while he lives. The sentence follows the reference to Paracel.; the note does not show whether the words are his or Croll's.

observations.quote: There is no perfection of things without the help of Divinity, and its demonstration.
observations.note: The note ends by saying nothing is perfected without divine help and its demonstration; whose words these are is not shown.

observations.quote: He that desireth this Art, must not be a slave to other mens judgment, nor live upon their purse, and must retire himselfe
observations.note: Three demands on the seeker: his own judgement, his own means, and withdrawal from company.

observations.quote: Too much acquantance hinder them / Who labour to find out this Gem.
observations.note: A verse couplet gives the reason for withdrawing: much acquaintance hinders the seeker. The thing sought is called a Gem. The verse carries no name.

observations.quote: Praebet amicorum, nil nisi copia damnum.
observations.note: A Latin line in the margin beside the English verse, making the same point: a crowd of friends brings only harm. No author is named.

observations.quote: doth hinder and much disturb the effect in any operation
observations.note: The faults of a companion (arrogant loquacity, incredulity, envy, infidelity, an Epicurean indignity) are said to hinder the effect of any operation.

observations.quote: Reverend antiquity, with one consent acknowledgeth that never any from the first man to the last could find ont the Divine secreu of that Art
observations.name: Reverend antiquity
observations.note: Given as the agreed word of antiquity: no one ever found the secret by natural wit, reason or experience (the words around 'Natural' are partly unread).

observations.quote: it is somthing Divine and hid, and that which is above Reason
observations.note: The reason given within antiquity's acknowledgement: the secret is divine, hidden and above reason.

observations.quote: those who have labored and toyled to find out this knowledg by dayly reading and comparing of Authors, do witnesse
observations.note: The long and fruitless toil of those who sought it by daily reading and comparing of authors is called as witness that it is not found so.

observations.quote: the glorious God and most blessed bestower of all graces hath reavealed and made it plaine to his faithfull wise ones
observations.note: Against that, God has revealed it and made it plain to his faithful wise ones who fear him, that they may praise him.

observations.quote: Ecclesiastic. 38.
observations.name: Ecclesiastic.
observations.note: The margin cites Ecclesiastic. 38 beside the words on God revealing it to his faithful wise ones.

observations.quote: when men seek the Kingdome of God, and study to finde out the Celestiall Stone in the last place
observations.note: The thing is named the Celestiall Stone. Several defensible readings: (a) it is to be sought only after the Kingdom of God (reader A); (b) men put the seeking of the Kingdom of God and the study of the stone last, a cause of their failure (reader B). The parenthesis does not settle it.

observations.quote: The one only and true way to all Secrets is to have recourse to God the author of all good, according to our Saviours command.
observations.note: The margin at the head of the paragraph: the one way to all secrets is recourse to God, as the Saviour commands.

observations.quote: there is not one to whom the doors of Nature are unlockt, and that hath the Divine bolt removed
observations.note: Among thousands who seek, not one has Nature's doors unlocked and the divine bolt drawn; God's will keeps the bolt in place.

observations.quote: who giveth his gifts to whom he will, and withdraweth them from whom be pleaseth
observations.note: The cause is placed in the will of God, who gives and withdraws his gifts as he pleases.

observations.quote: it is not expedient for all to their salvation, that they should have Honors & riches with their health
observations.note: God withholds it because honours and riches together with health would not serve every man's salvation.

observations.quote: the key of the Phylosophicall Garden (as I know some that have)
observations.what: the key of the Phylosophicall Garden
observations.note: Some may get the key of the philosophical garden, and Croll says he knows some who have, yet without grace they cannot open the gate or enter.

observations.quote: because the Gate was bolted, that is, the Divine Grace and Benediction was denyed and did resist
observations.note: Stated: the text itself glosses the bolted gate ('that is') as divine grace and blessing denied.

observations.quote: gather those desired fruits of the Hermetick Tree, and eate the most sweet kernells of this mystery
observations.note: What such men could not do is put in a figure of gathering the fruit of the Hermetick Tree and eating the kernels of the mystery.

observations.quote: having got the most true Phylosophycall Ferment or Leaven (but prepar'd by others) have not been able to improve or multiply it any further
observations.note: A named stage: a true philosophical ferment or leaven, to be improved or multiplied; impostors of Croll's age holding one prepared by others could not, for ignorance of 'the principle or beginning'.

observations.quote: this most holy science never admitted any such unskilfull Thraso's into its inner rooms
observations.note: The science is said to keep such men out of its inner rooms.

observations.quote: This is that work that is hid under the robe of the Phylosophicall Virgin, which even one brother would not teach another
observations.note: The work is hidden under the robe of the Phylosophicall Virgin and not taught even from brother to brother.

observations.quote: it is to no purpose to tempt an Adept Phylosopher with promises of rewards, favour, or any other kind of respects that can be imagined, to part with it
observations.note: No reward or favour will bring an adept philosopher to part with it.

observations.quote: which even one brother would not teach another
observations.note: Here the work is not taught even to a brother; CH6.12 names a wise master's ocular demonstration as one of two ways to the gift, and N258 entrance by word of mouth from one who has the secret and teaches it while he lives.

observations.quote: This is that Secret laid up and buryed in the most secret Treasury of the Mind and Memory
observations.note: The secret is kept in mind and memory.

observations.quote: doe study and strive to be harsh and rugged, least they should disclose their more abstruse or dark sence to any, and expose the most noble Gemm of this Science to hogs and swine
observations.note: The philosophers the text calls genuine and more occult write harshly and roughly on purpose, so that their dark sense is not disclosed and the gem not cast to swine.

observations.quote: God would not manifest this knowledg to all, to avoyd offence.
observations.note: The margin gives God's reason for the hiding: not to show this knowledge to all, to avoid offence.

observations.quote: have in a wise and ingenious craft covenanted and sworn they would never write it plainly in any Book
observations.note: The philosophers are said to have bound themselves by covenant and oath never to write it plainly in any book.

observations.quote: Nor hath any of them who kept this knowledge in the secret of their heart, made it known to any but such who had an understanding allegorically
observations.note: It has been made known only to those who understand allegorically.

observations.quote: because they are made Lords of Things, they should also have power to dispence or give Names at their pleasure
observations.note: The philosophers have liberty to give names as they please and to 'cloath their children as they listed': the text warns that the names in their writings are of their own choosing. Interpreted (reader B's): the children are the things they name; the lines do not say so.

observations.quote: This is not believed, but being proved with the gain of labor, toyl and hazard, it is made plain toward the end which proveth the work.
observations.note: The thing is not believed until proved by labour, toil and hazard; it becomes plain toward the end that proves the work.

observations.quote: On this the hinge of the whole busines turneth, as Gold animated by the Salt of Niture is made the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
observations.what: the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
observations.note: The margin names what the whole business turns on and gives, as its likeness or instance, gold animated by 'the Salt of Niture' (so spelled) as the chief subject of the philosophers' metallic physick.

observations.quote: Gold animated by the Salt of Niture is made the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
observations.note: The margin puts gold at the centre of the philosophers' metallic physick, while CH6.11 has the seekers leave 'the mettalls' to the greedy. Several readings: CH6.11 may concern seeking metals for wealth only; the lines do not settle it.

observations.quote: Though True Phylosophers exactly & with greatest ingenuity, have mutually ingag'd and set themselves upon one and the same thing
observations.note: The true philosophers are all said to be set upon one and the same thing.

observations.quote: in their precepts, as in a glasse, it hath been sufficiently made known to men of a wise understanding
observations.note: Their precepts show it, as in a glass, sufficiently, but only to the wise, chosen of God, worthy and sworn in the Art.

observations.quote: Neverthelesse religously affirming, that none can attaine the desired end
observations.name: True Phylosophers
observations.note: What follows on the joining of two things is given as the true philosophers' own affirmation: without it no one reaches the desired end.

observations.quote: though they sleight all particulars, which naturally doe altogether want the virtue of tincturing, unlesse they proceed from the first fountaine
observations.note: Inside that affirmation: things called particulars lack the power of tincturing unless they come from 'the first fountaine'.

observations.quote: before the fat or blood of the Sun and the Dew of the Lunary, be joyned into one body by the circular wheel of the Elements with the help of Art and Nature in the form of an Hexagon
observations.note: The step named as needful: the fat or blood of the Sun and the Dew of the Lunary joined into one body by the circular wheel of the Elements, by art and nature, in the form of an Hexagon. The words are covered ones and the lines given do not open them.

observations.quote: Read Gen. 1.27, 28. Hermes his Table, Morienes, Alan. Rodargir. Monad.
observations.name: Gen.; Hermes; Morienes; Alan.; Rodargir.; Monad.; T...evisan.; Lull.
observations.note: Beside the joining in the form of an Hexagon the margin lists writings and persons to read: Gen. 1.27, 28, Hermes his Table, Morienes, Alan., Rodargir., Monad., a partly illegible 'T...evisan.', and Lull.

observations.quote: which can never be done except the most High God please, who alone of his speciall mercy graciously bestoweth this singular gift of the Holy Spirit
observations.note: The joining cannot be done unless God pleases; the gift is called a gift of the Holy Spirit.

observations.quote: let that man use what Arts soever he can, yet shall he never get any thing against the Will of God
observations.note: Here a man to whom God gives none of his treasures never gets anything, whatever arts he uses; CH6.19 tells of impostors who by unlawful means had got the true ferment, though they could not multiply it.

observations.quote: for the Spirit proceedeth from Grace, who inspireth whom he will
observations.note: The paragraph closes on grace: whoever God denies cannot gain it by any art, for the Spirit inspires whom he will.

observations.quote: Seeing therefore all mans endeavor is but vaine except God prosper it
observations.note: Croll's conclusion: human effort is vain unless God prospers it.

observations.quote: Levit. 26.20.
observations.name: Levit.
observations.note: The margin cites Levit. 26.20 beside the words on vain endeavour and God as moderator of the universe.

observations.quote: should suffer themselves to be cheated and deceived, with the greedy world by the golden promises of circumforaneous, vitious, and most lying Impostors
observations.note: Croll wonders that many great men of his age, wasting time and estates, let themselves be cheated by the golden promises of wandering impostors.

observations.quote: without the liberall and right noble arts (of which those Phylosophists and Imposters are altogether destitute, having not tasted so much as a drop of the Springs of Nature) no perfect perception of Mysteries can be attained to
observations.note: Without the liberal and noble arts no perfect perception of mysteries is reached; the impostors, also called Phylosophists, lack those arts wholly.

observations.quote: Great men commit great errours.
observations.note: A saying in the margin beside the words on great men who are cheated.

observations.name: Psal.; Prov.; Wisd.; Eccl.
observations.note: The same note lists four places of scripture beside the passage on deceived great men.

observations.quote: Those Gymnosophists with their Fantasticall and Frantick inventions, inrich the eares of credulous men that they may make their pockets poor
observations.note: The same deceivers, here named 'Gymnosophists', fill the ears of the credulous to empty their pockets.

observations.quote: whose company we should avoyd even as the most raging torments of hell
observations.note: Croll's counsel: avoid the impostors' company.

observations.quote: the Wisdome of the Lord, whose mysterie is onely with them that Fear him
observations.note: The mystery of the Lord's wisdom is only with those who fear him; it does not enter the souls of deceivers.

observations.quote: with their guilfull devices of painting white and red, and pargetting womens faces
observations.note: The deceivers' devices are painting white and red and plastering women's faces. Several defensible readings: (a) plainly, cosmetics; (b) a figure for a false show of colour laid on the surface, which CH6.25 supports where they find 'only the colour' in place of the Tincture. The lines do not settle it.

observations.quote: Great gaine is the scope of sophisticall craft, because Dust & Ashes is the end of such smock-sellers.
observations.note: The margin says sophistical craft aims at gain and ends in dust and ashes; it calls its men smock-sellers, a word the lines do not explain.

observations.quote: playing away and losing the story of Pandora
observations.note: The deceivers' loss is put as playing away and losing 'the story of Pandora'; the lines do not explain the figure.

observations.quote: instead of the Tincture they should find only the colour, instead of the Hermetick Stone a pibble or glasse, and instead of great Treasure and riches nothing but coals and ashes
observations.name: Alphidius
observations.note: Given as what Alphidius foretold for such men; his words set the true things (the Tincture, the Hermetick Stone, treasure) against what they get (colour, a pebble or glass, coals and ashes).

observations.quote: this efficacious transmutatory virtue of these Impostors, which makes wise men fools, strong men weak, rich men poor
observations.note: Ironical: the word for the power of changing is turned on the impostors, whose only 'transmutatory virtue' changes men for the worse.

observations.quote: Piety is the most necessary key to the knowledge of all Secrets.
observations.note: The margin at the head of the paragraph names piety as the key most needed for knowing any secret.

observations.quote: See Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS his verse
observations.name: Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a verse of Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS (its place partly unread) against those who rush into 'the Vestry of Phylosophy'.

observations.quote: It is not expedient to reveal it to any carnall man, because thou wilt be accuised for making known so great a Secret.
observations.note: A warning against revealing it to a carnal man, on pain of a curse ('accuised' as printed). The note does not show whose words these are.

observations.quote: He that publisheth this Art, let him die an evill death, saith Lully, because it is a secret to be given and revealed by God alone who hath created Nature, and no other
observations.name: Lully
observations.note: Given as Lully's words: a curse on whoever publishes the Art, because the secret is God's alone to reveal, to whom he will.

observations.name: Job; Prov.; Apoc.; Es.; Jer.; Ezek.
observations.note: The note ends with a list of places of scripture.

observations.quote: the envy of Phylosophers is not against the Children of Art and Science, who seek not their own but Gods glory
observations.note: The philosophers' 'envy', the word used here for their withholding, is not turned against worthy seekers who seek God's glory.

observations.quote: he that is an Adept and compleat Phylosopher, a keeper of Gods Secrets, and is conformed to the dignification of his work
observations.what: an Adept and compleat Phylosopher, a keeper of Gods Secrets
observations.note: The adept is set apart as a complete philosopher and a keeper of God's secrets.

observations.quote: after he by the Blessing of God hath happily labored like Hermes more then twenty years
observations.note: The adept's labour is put at more than twenty years, likened to that of Hermes.

observations.quote: will be lesse afraid to die an hundred most cruell deaths, and indure all manner of miseries and punishment
observations.note: The adept would sooner die a hundred deaths than publish the treasure to the wicked or the unworthy.

observations.quote: this greatest and richest Terrene Treasure, the Perfect Benefit or good gift of GOD
observations.what: this greatest and richest Terrene Treasure; the Perfect Benefit or good gift of GOD
observations.note: The secret is named the greatest earthly treasure and God's perfect gift, come down from the Father of Lights.

observations.quote: which Secret would by evill men, with the ruine of the whole world, be abused
observations.note: A reason for keeping it: evil men would abuse the secret, to the ruin of the whole world.

observations.quote: except he can give a good account of his Stewardship and the Talent committed to him
observations.note: The adept holds the secret as a steward and must answer for the talent entrusted at the last judgement, on pain of his soul.

observations.quote: the heat of the Centre united to the heat of Sun shall set all corruption of the Elements on fire
observations.note: At the last day the heat of the centre joined with the heat of the Sun shall set the corruption of the elements on fire.

observations.quote: when every evill and impure thing shall be cast like lead with the damned into Hell
observations.note: Every evil and impure thing is then cast into hell; the likeness used is lead.

observations.quote: with unquenchable brimston like molten glasse, continually burning and never wasting
observations.note: The torment is by brimstone, likened to molten glass, that burns without consuming.

observations.quote: The property of fire is to seperate the impurity of the Elements.
observations.note: The margin states a property of fire: it separates the impurity of the elements, in line with the purging said of the medicine in CH6.1.

observations.quote: Apoc. 20.10. The end of the world is by fire. There is a Sea of glass mingled with fire. Apoc. 15.2.
observations.name: Apoc.
observations.note: Two places in Apoc. are cited, for the end of the world by fire and for a sea of glass mingled with fire, beside the paragraph's molten glass.

observations.quote: Read Isa. Holand in opere minerali.
observations.name: Isa. Holand
observations.note: The note sends the reader to Isa. Holand's mineral work, and names a place in Rom., beside the passage on the world's end by fire.

voices.quote: as if they were but the speculations of idle men
voices.basis: the view of those who revile them 'as the most doe', reported in order to reject it

voices.quote: which the ignorant basely and wretchedly condemn of falshood
voices.basis: the judgement of 'the ignorant', reported in order to reject it
follows 'See Paracel.' to the end of the note; whether Paracelsus's words or the author's is not shown
verse couplet introduced by 'For', no speaker named

voices.quote: Praebet amicorum, nil nisi copia damnum.
voices.basis: Latin verse line beside the couplet, no author named

voices.quote: Reverend antiquity, with one consent acknowledgeth that
voices.basis: 'acknowledgeth that ... But that ...' governs the rest of the sentence to 'for ever and ever'

voices.quote: Neverthelesse religously affirming, that none can attaine the desired end
voices.basis: 'religously affirming, that', said of the True Phylosophers; runs to 'when he seeth good'

voices.quote: that when their braines grow giddy
voices.basis: 'what Alphidius foretold should happen to them'

voices.quote: It is not expedient to reveal it to any carnall man
voices.basis: addressed to 'thou'; stands before 'saith Lully' but the note does not show whether it is Lully's

voices.quote: He that publisheth this Art, let him die an evill death
voices.basis: 'saith Lully'; runs to 'not of any mortal Man'
